You are comparing two drafts written from the same brief. Read no other file, and do not run commands or browse; judge only the text below.

Brief: Write the landing page copy for `portlog`, following the tool page section order.

<<<DRAFT A
# See which process held a local TCP port

portlog records local TCP port history, so you can look back after a process exits.

```sh
brew install example/tap/portlog
```

macOS and Linux · Written in Go · MIT license

```sh
portlog who 3000
```

What was on port 3000 an hour ago?

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `portlog start` | Run the background recorder. |
| `portlog stop` | Stop the recorder. |
| `portlog who 3000` | Show every process that held port 3000, newest first. |
| `portlog free 3000` | Stop the process holding port 3000 now, after confirmation. |

## Keys

| Option | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--since 2h` | Limit history to the last two hours: `portlog who 3000 --since 2h`. |
| `-y` | Skip confirmation: `portlog free 3000 -y`. |

## History

portlog keeps seven days of history in `~/.portlog/`.

## Good to know

**Command-line arguments**

portlog never records command-line arguments, because they can hold secrets.

<<<DRAFT B
# See which process held a port

portlog records which process held each local TCP port over time. Use it to answer “what was on port 3000 an hour ago?” after the process has exited.

```sh
brew install example/tap/portlog
```

macOS and Linux · Written in Go · MIT license

Start recording, then look up port 3000:

```sh
portlog start
portlog who 3000
```

## Commands

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `portlog start` | Runs a background recorder. |
| `portlog stop` | Stops the recorder. |
| `portlog who 3000` | Shows every process that held port 3000, newest first. |
| `portlog who 3000 --since 2h` | Limits the history to the last two hours. |
| `portlog free 3000` | Stops the process that holds port 3000 now, after confirmation. |

To skip the confirmation, use `portlog free 3000 -y`.

## Good to know

### History

portlog keeps history for 7 days in `~/.portlog/`.

### Command-line arguments

portlog never records command-line arguments, because they can hold secrets.

items.title: Thinking
items.text:
I'm reviewing draft A: the headline is fine, but the `portlog who 3000` example skips `portlog start`, so a new reader would get nothing back. The question after the code block and the "Keys" heading also read awkwardly, and `who 3000` without `--since 1h` doesn't really answer "an hour ago." I can't tell yet where the section order lands on the tool page.

Between the two drafts, A's section order (Commands, Keys, History, Good to know) doesn't match B's, and "Keys" may just be a convention for terminal-UI tools. A's "Good to know" block with a lone bold label reads awkwardly. B walks through start and then who, so a reader gets a result, and its headline drops "TCP" while the body keeps it. On balance B comes out ahead.

{"reader": "B", "careful": "B", "overall": "B", "reason": "B's quick start runs `portlog start` before `portlog who 3000`, so a first-time reader actually gets history; A's quick start skips the recorder, leaves its 'an hour ago' question hanging after the code block, and puts command-line options under an odd 'Keys' heading."}
